name: Wei Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, Wei. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to companies, unions, parties or government. What you say is confidential. Could you start by telling me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm learning to run the winder at the Grayson shaft, the zinc mine north of town. The winder is the big engine that raises and lowers the cage, the lift that takes the men a kilometre and a half down, and the skips that bring the ore up. Most of it runs on automatic now, but the safety rules still say a qualified person sits in the chair when people are in the cage. I'm not qualified yet; I sit next to Gareth, who's been doing it for thirty years, and I take over when he lets me. It's calm work, but you never forget there are forty men hanging on that rope.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to the winder?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I had the family hardware shop on Mill Street for twenty-five years, my father's before me. A big warehouse store opened by the highway and that was that. I closed it myself, paid every supplier, and I didn't ask anybody for a handout. That took our savings, so now we've maybe three weeks in the bank. The mine took me on at fifty-five, and my son-in-law, who's an electrician there, put a word in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI Plateau. That suits me. I'd finish my training and the robots would stay in the brochure for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the shaft head I'd say the winder's been mostly automatic for years and it still needs a man in the chair, so nothing's changed. I'd say it to Gareth over the flask. I don't go in for talk on the internet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I can finish my training, get certified and work to sixty-five, if I pass. Gareth retires in three years, and if I'm not qualified by then, they'll bring someone in from outside and I'm back on the surface crew at less money. We've three weeks in the bank, so the certificate is the whole plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd study the rule book every night, with the AI quizzing me now and then, and aim to pass the winder exam within a year. I'd start putting twenty a week aside again. And I'd keep doing the odd weekend repair with my son-in-law, cash in hand, for the gas bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a way I can work with. It's exam nerves more than fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if you don't pass?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I've wasted Gareth's patience and my son-in-law's good word, and that weighs on me more than the money. The surface crew pays about eighty a week less. We'd manage, the way we managed after the shop, but I'd feel it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does your wife see it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My wife does the sums with me every Sunday, on paper, at the kitchen table. My wife says a man who closed his shop owing nobody a penny can pass a winder exam. She has more faith in me than the examiners will.

If I'm not qualified when **Gareth retires**, I'm back on the surface crew at less money.
With **three weeks** in the bank, the certificate is the whole plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Checking and planning. That's what I do in the chair, if I'm honest: watch the screens and decide when to stop. The hands-on bit is pressing the button.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the shaft head I'd say the safety rules on the winder won't change in a hurry, whatever the computers can do. I'd tell the young ones to learn a trade with their hands. That's what I'd say out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, a man in the winder chair is there to watch and decide, and that's the thinking work your card says goes first. The only thing between me and a computer in the winder chair is a line in the safety rules. Rules do change, just slowly. If they change it in three or four years, I'd be sixty-two, three years short of my pension, with three weeks in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hurry the certificate, because a qualified man is the last to go, and I'd save fifty a week by cutting the newspaper and the car trips. I'd ask the shaft foreman about the rope inspection crew as a fallback, since that's hands-on work. And I'd learn whatever new system they bring in, once I've seen it working at another mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's the waiting I don't like, reading the safety bulletins every month to see if the rule has moved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Gareth?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gareth would say the chair's safe till he retires and that's all he cares about, and he'd be joking, mostly. I'd ask Gareth to teach me every trick he knows anyway. A man who knows the old way is useful when the new way breaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your son-in-law's word still help you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It got me in the door. It won't keep me in the chair if a rule changes. My son-in-law is an electrician, so he'll be fine, and that's one less worry for my daughter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking work in 2028. Well. Sitting in the winder chair is thinking work, if you're honest about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At church coffee I'd say the rules on carrying men down a shaft won't change overnight, whatever the computers can do. I'd say a sensible company keeps a person in the chair. And I'd say young men should learn a trade with their hands, because that's got a few more years in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the winder already runs itself, and what I do in the chair is watch and decide when to stop it. That's exactly the work a thinking computer could do in 2028. The only thing in the way is the rule book, and if the machine really is as good as a person, somebody in an office will sign the paper sooner than I'd like. I'd be sixty, five years short of my pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still pass the certificate this year, because a qualified man is the last to go. But I'd also ask the shaft foreman if I could join the crew that inspects the rope and greases the sheaves, because that's hands-on work that lasts till 2031. We'd cut everything extra and put about fifty a week aside. And I'd do weekend repair jobs with my son-in-law, taps and fences and door hinges, the things I used to sell parts for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd keep it in my chest. Like the day the warehouse store opened and I still had a full shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Gareth do if the chair went to a computer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gareth would retire that day, he's sixty-one and he's said so. He'd shake my hand and tell me the rope crew is honest work. And he'd be right, but I'd miss the chair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd still pass the certificate. Why, if the chair might go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I don't know when the rule book changes, and nobody else does either. If the rule book holds till 2031, the certificate is my wage. If it doesn't, at least I've finished something, which matters to me after the shop.

Young men should learn **a hands-on trade**, because that's got a few more years in it.
think: In the chair I **watch and decide** when to stop, exactly what a thinking computer could do in 2028.
Only **the rule book** stands in the way, and I'd be sixty, five years short of my pension.

S2.quote: Sitting in the winder chair is thinking work, if you're honest about it.
fieldNote: Wei saw that his job looks like machine work but is really **watching and deciding**.

steps.text: Ask to join the Grayson rope inspection crew, which lasts until 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2031 for the thinking. I'd be sixty-three. Pension at sixty-five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people have time to prepare, and they should get on with it instead of complaining. At church I'd say look after your families and learn something solid. That's what I'd tell anybody.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd make it. The chair could go in 2031, but the rule book always lags a few years, and the rope crew lasts till 2034. If the rule book buys me two years and my son-in-law's toolbox buys me one more, I'm there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the certificate this year and work every shift I can, saving about sixty a week. I'd do weekend repair jobs with my son-in-law. And I'd keep using the AI to study, a bit more than now, because by 2031 I'd want to understand what's replacing me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but it's a manageable worry. I can count the years on one hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why learn about the thing that's replacing you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if they keep one man to watch the computer, I want it to be me. And my father taught me it’s better to understand a new tool than to be afraid of it. He said that about every tool in the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Lucia say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lucia would say stop counting and go to sleep. Then she'd count with me. She's better at it than I am.

S3.quote: My father taught me it’s better to understand a new tool than to be afraid of it.

steps.text: Get the winder certificate and save about sixty a week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2036. I'd be sixty-eight. Retired three years by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time for everybody to get ready, and young people should take apprenticeships now. I'd say it at church coffee. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be fine. I'd finish my certificate, work the chair to sixty-five and hand it on. By 2036 the winder can run itself, and I'll be teaching my grandson to fix a dripping tap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working, finish the winder certificate and save a little each month. When a new system comes in, I'd learn it with everyone else. No big moves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit sad for Gareth's kind of work, that's all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why sad for Gareth's kind of work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a winderman is trusted with forty lives, and that trust goes to a computer. I'm not against it if it's safer. I'm just sorry nobody will be proud of that job any more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the shop still be on your mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Always a little. I'd like to finish at the mine owing nobody, the way I closed the shop. With ten years, I think I can.

Young people should take **apprenticeships** now, while there's time to learn properly.
think: I'd finish my certificate, work the chair **to sixty-five** and hand it on.
By 2036 the winder runs itself, and I'll be teaching **my grandson** to fix a dripping tap.

feel: **Calm**, with some **sadness** for the old pride of the winderman's job.
S4.quote: By 2036 the winder can run itself, and I'll be teaching my grandson to fix a dripping tap.
fieldNote: With the long timeline Wei **retires first** and is calm.
He mourns **the trust and pride** of the winderman's job, not the wage.
Finishing **debt-free** remains his measure of a good working life.

steps.text: Finish the winder certificate and work the chair to sixty-five

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because a thinking computer could take the winder chair in 2028, and I'd be five years short of the pension with nothing in the bank. What would help is the company keeping people like me on to the pension in some job, even sweeping, and proper apprenticeships for the young ones. I don't want a cheque for nothing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask what people are proud of. I closed my shop owing nobody a penny. I'd like to finish at the mine the same way, owing nobody and on my own two feet. That matters to men like me.

headlineQuote: I closed my shop owing nobody a penny. I'd like to finish at the mine the same way, owing nobody and on my own two feet.
portrait: Wei Rossi, 58, is training to run **the winder** at the Grayson zinc mine, the engine that raises and lowers the cage.
He closed his family hardware shop **owing nobody**, which left about three weeks of savings.
In a plateau he's **uneasy**, with everything riding on qualifying before his mentor Gareth retires.
Steady change makes him **anxious**: watching the winder is thinking work, kept human only by safety rules.
AGI by 2028 keeps him **anxious**; with more time he expects to reach his pension, sad for the winderman's lost pride.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because a thinking computer could take the winder chair when he's five years short of the pension.
whatWouldHelp: The company **keeping older workers** on until their pension in some job, even sweeping.
**Proper apprenticeships** for young people rather than cheques for nothing.
